title: Caring for the First Teeth
hook: Baby teeth matter — they hold space for adult teeth and shape eating and speech. Brushing starts with the very first tooth, and the first dental visit comes earlier than most parents expect.
key_points: Start brushing as soon as the first tooth appears: twice a day with a soft brush and a tiny smear (rice-grain size) of fluoride toothpaste.
Before teeth, wipe the gums with a clean, damp cloth to get a baby used to mouth care.
Book the first dental visit by the first birthday — or within 6 months of the first tooth, whichever comes first.
Avoid putting a baby to bed with a bottle of milk or juice; pooled sugar on the teeth overnight causes early decay.
content_html: It's easy to think baby teeth don't count because they fall out anyway, but they do real work: they let a child chew, help shape speech, and hold space so the adult teeth come in straight. Caring for them starts surprisingly early. Even before any teeth appear, wiping a baby's gums with a clean, damp cloth gets them used to having their mouth cleaned.
extra_html: Once that first tooth pokes through, begin brushing twice a day with a soft baby toothbrush and just a smear of fluoride toothpaste — about the size of a grain of rice (a pea-sized amount comes later, around age three). The other early step parents often miss is timing the first dental visit: the recommendation is by the first birthday, or within six months of the first tooth. A big preventable cause of early decay is the bedtime bottle — when milk or juice pools on the teeth through the night, it feeds the bacteria that cause cavities, so keep sugary drinks out of the crib. This is general guidance; your pediatrician or dentist can tailor a routine to your child.

related.title: Teething: Signs and Safe Soothing
related.hook: Teething often starts around 6 months, but the timing varies a lot. Expect drooling, gum-rubbing, and fussiness — not a high fever, which points to something else.

related.title: Well-Child Visits: Your Regular Check-Ups
related.hook: Well-child visits aren't just for when something's wrong — they track growth and development, deliver vaccines on schedule, and catch problems early, even when your child seems perfectly fine.

flashcards.prompt: When should you start brushing a baby's teeth?

choices.text: As soon as the first tooth appears, twice a day with a rice-grain smear of fluoride toothpaste
Only once all the baby teeth are in

flashcards.explanation_html: Brushing begins with the first tooth — twice daily with a soft brush and a tiny (rice-grain) smear of fluoride toothpaste.

flashcards.prompt: By when should a child have their first dental visit?

choices.text: By the first birthday, or within 6 months of the first tooth
Around age 3, when they can sit still
Only if a tooth looks discolored

flashcards.explanation_html: The recommendation is a first dental visit by age one, or within six months of the first tooth coming in — whichever is first.

flashcards.prompt: Why avoid a bottle of milk or juice in bed?
flashcards.back_html: Sugars from milk or juice pool on the teeth overnight, feeding the bacteria that cause early childhood tooth decay. Offer the bottle before bed, not in it.
